newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end lower after German news.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end lower after German news.

text.p: COMEX gold and silver ended lower Wednesday, after news near the close that some members of the German governing coalition were considering using Bundesbank gold to help Germany meet the criteria for joining the European Monetary Union (EMU).

But NYMEX platinum group metals (PGMs) held onto most of the sessions gains, after palladium saw new contract highs, despite news this week that Russian exports of PGMs would resume in June after a five month suspension.

"Germany is unlikely to actually sell any gold, as it has repeatedly denied it would do so, and is one of the few remaining countries to oppose the sale of IMF gold sales," said Ted Kempf, analyst with New York-based industry consultants, CPM Group.
German government sources said Wednesday the government was considering using Bundesbank gold reserves for budgetary purposes, confirming details of a German newspaper report.

According to an advance copy of a report to appear in Thursday's "Handelsblatt" newspaper the use of Bundesbank gold was being urged by members of the FDP (Free Democratic Party), the junior partner in the German government coalition, to avoid tax increases.
Germany, like many other EU countries, is struggling to reduce its budget deficit to 3.0 percent of GDP, one of the criteria that must be met for membership in the EMU in 1999.
Earlier the EU in Brussels ruled that the sale of assets such as gold reserves could not be used to reduce a budget deficit, but could be used to reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio.
But the newspaper report did not say Germany would actually sell gold outright, only that the gold reserves would be revalued to market prices and used to "finance investments", analysts noted.
As recently as April 16 German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told the German parliaments finance committee that Germany had no plans to sell gold.

But last month Waigel did tell the German parliamentary budget committee that Germany's gold reserves, currently valued at around 17 billion marks ($9.8 billion), should instead be valued nearer to their market value of around 70 billion marks, according to the German newsweekly "Focus" on April 26.
Official German gold reserves stand at about 3,700 tonnes (118,958,700 ounces), according to London-based industry consultants, Gold Field Mineral Services Ltd.

"Even if the German's do not actually sell any gold, mobilizing German gold reserves is another sea change in thinking, like the Swiss move to mobilize their gold reserves recently, and could send gold prices down toward $300 an ounce," one New York bullion banker said.
Last month Switzerland announced a planned fund to compensate Holocaust victims which would be financed by revaluing, and selling some of the Swiss National Bank's gold reserves.

COMEX June gold ended down $2.30 an ounce at $348.20, after first ignoring the low-inflation implications of the fall in the U.S. April producer price index of 0.6 percent, and trading up to a session high at $350.80.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $346.80/30, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $349.10 an ounce, and the New York close Tuesday around $349.25/75.
COMEX July silver ended down 4.0 cents at $4.838 an ounce, after trading a $4.895-4.830 range.
But silver's fundamentals remain better than gold's, with no threat of central bank silver sales hanging over the market, analysts said.

Above-ground stocks of silver continue to be eroded by the ongoing deficit between mine production and scrap supply on the one hand, and fabrication demand on the other, industry consultants Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS) said in its 1997 report on the silver market published Wednesday.

"The evidence suggests the market is moving in the direction of a genuine tightening, with identifiable stocks now approximately equal to four years of the supply/demand gap recorded in 1996," GFMS analyst Philip Klapwijk said.

NYMEX July platinum closed up $1.90 at $393.80 an ounce, just below Monday's 10-week highs at $397.50, and NYMEX June palladium ended up $2.35 an ounce at $173.90, after climbing to a new contract high at $175.00.
Russia's metal export agency, Almaz, confirmed this week it was in talks with customers over new supply contracts for PGM's and said exports should resume again in June.

But after five months of disruption to Russian PGM exports, it would take some time for confidence to be restored and PGM prices were likely to see higher prices until the supply pipeline was refilled, analysts said.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
